title: What if you could see with sound, like a bat?

narration.heading: Seeing with sound
narration.text: You wake up in total darkness. Then you click your tongue, and the room appears.

narration.heading: How bats do it
narration.text: Bats do this every night. They call out, then listen for the echo bouncing back.

narration.heading: The echo map
narration.text: The delay tells them how far away things are. Two ears tell them which way.

narration.heading: Too high for you
narration.text: Most of their calls are too high for you to hear. Your ears top out around twenty thousand hertz.

narration.heading: Loud and high
narration.text: Some bats call at over two hundred thousand. Some calls hit a hundred and forty decibels.

narration.heading: The buzz
narration.text: Closing in on an insect, a bat speeds up to two hundred clicks a second. A buzz.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? People can do this too. Some blind people echolocate with tongue clicks.

narration.heading: Daniel Kish
narration.text: Daniel Kish lost both eyes as a baby. Clicking, he leads blind teens on hikes and mountain-bike rides.

beats.label: old when he lost his eyes

narration.heading: Seeing, really
narration.text: In expert echolocators, echoes even light up the brain's vision area. Would you learn to see with sound?

skit.text: Echolocation? I just ping the router and hope.

titles: What if you could see with sound, like a bat?
Some people really can see with sound
youtube.description: How bats build a map of the dark from echoes, why you can't hear most of their calls, and the blind people who learned to echolocate with tongue clicks.

sources.claim: Echolocating animals call and listen for echoes; ranging comes from the time delay between call and echo, and two ears give direction; bat calls range from 11 kHz to 212 kHz at 60–140 dB; call rates rise to as high as 200 clicks per second in the terminal buzz
Human hearing is commonly given as 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz

Some blind people echolocate with tongue clicks; Daniel Kish had his eyes removed at 13 months and leads blind teenagers on hikes and mountain-bike rides; a 2014 study found echoes activated the primary visual cortex of blind expert echolocators
